documents.title: Call from daughter
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Daughter called (on HIPAA form as health care proxy). Worried about her father for about a month: stays in bed most of the day, stopped going out to the garden, doesn't watch the games anymore, she has to remind him to eat and shower. He has lost weight, clothes loose. She asked him directly if he has thought about hurting himself and he said no. No confusion, no falls, no new medicines she knows of. He agreed to come in. Offered tomorrow 10:00 with PCP; she will bring him. Advised if he says anything about wanting to die or she can't wake him, call 911 or 988. PCP aware.

events.reason: Low mood and withdrawal, weight loss

conditions.label: Major depressive disorder, single episode, severe without psychotic features

medications.sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth at bedtime

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, high MDM

documents.title: Office Visit: mood
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Here with daughter, who called yesterday.

HPI: Over roughly the last month Paul has pulled away from everything. He hasn't been out to start the garden, which his daughter says is unheard of in March, and he stopped watching football with his neighbor. Most days he is in bed until afternoon. He needs reminding to eat and to shower. He falls asleep fine but is up around 3 in the morning and lies there until it gets light. He describes himself as "tired of everything." Asked directly: no thoughts of suicide, no plan, never attempted, no guns in the house. No hallucinations. Weight down 5 kg in about 3 weeks by our scale. No change in cardiac symptoms, no chest pain, no dyspnea. No new medicines, no alcohol increase (hasn't had a beer in weeks). No prior episodes of depression that he or his daughter can recall. Couldn't name a trigger. He does still walk the dog, briefly, because "she won't let me not."

PHQ-9: 21. Answered item 9 as 0.

Exam: vitals within normal limits, weight as charted. Thin, slumped in the chair, poor eye contact, speech slowed with long latency, flat affect. Oriented, follows the conversation, recall 3/3. Thyroid not enlarged. Heart regular. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, no mass. No edema.

Assessment: Major depressive disorder, single episode, severe, without psychotic features: neurovegetative symptoms, psychomotor slowing and weight loss, no SI. Rule out medical contributors.

Plan:
- CBC, CMP, TSH, B12 today.
- Start mirtazapine 15 mg at bedtime: should help sleep and appetite, and sits well with his heart medicines. Reviewed sedation, that benefit takes weeks.
- Offered referral to counseling; he declined for now, "let's see if the pill works." Will revisit.
- Safety: daughter staying over a few nights this week. 988 and our after-hours line given to both. Daughter will text me if anything changes.
- Video check in 2 weeks, visit in 6 weeks. Daily weights not needed; weekly is fine.

55 minutes spent, more than half counseling and coordination.

documents.title: Lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Paul (and hello to your daughter, who I know reads these). Your blood work came back normal: blood count, kidneys, liver, salts and calcium, thyroid and B12. That is reassuring that nothing physical is driving how you've been feeling. Keep taking the mirtazapine every night. Our video visit is on the 18th.

documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Came alone today, drove himself. Six weeks on mirtazapine 15 mg. Sleep good. Appetite back, weight up a bit. Up and dressed by mid-morning most days. Put in tomatoes last weekend with his daughter's help but says it felt like a chore. Still flat in the evenings. Denies SI.

AWV, subsequent.

Interval: depressive episode this spring, now much improved on mirtazapine 30 mg. Brought me a bag of peppers. Gardening, walking, back to the Sunday games with his neighbor. Sleep good.
PHQ-9: 5. No SI.

HRA: independent in ADLs/IADLs, drives, no falls, no hearing or vision complaints beyond readers. Lives alone with dog, daughter close by. Alcohol 1-2/wk. Former smoker.
Cognition: Mini-Cog normal.

Problems: CAD s/p LAD stent 2020 with stable angina; HTN; hyperlipidemia; OA knees; MDD single episode, now partial remission; former smoker.
Meds: aspirin 81, atorvastatin 40 qhs, metoprolol succinate 50, lisinopril 20, mirtazapine 30 qhs, acetaminophen prn. NKDA.

Exam: vitals reviewed, weight back near baseline. Brighter, good eye contact. Heart regular, lungs clear, no edema.

Prevention: colon UTD to 2028. LDCT due next month, ordered. Shingrix complete. Tdap 2022. PCV20 2021. Flu, updated COVID and RSV vaccine next month (discussed RSV for 60+ with heart disease; he wants it).
Labs: CMP, lipids, CBC, A1c.

A/P: MDD now partial remission, continue mirtazapine 30 mg at least through spring, then reassess. Other chronic problems stable. RTC 4 months.

LOW-DOSE CT CHEST, ANNUAL SCREENING
Comparison: 10/25/2022 and 10/19/2021.
Findings: Lungs clear without nodules. No consolidation or effusion. Central airways patent. No adenopathy. Normal heart size, no pericardial effusion. Coronary calcification with LAD stent, stable. Visualized upper abdomen unremarkable.

conditions.label: Second degree atrioventricular block, Mobitz type I

reports.text: Sinus rhythm with second-degree AV block, Mobitz type I: progressive PR prolongation with intermittently dropped QRS complexes, grouped beating. Ventricular rate 38. Narrow QRS. No acute ST-segment changes.
reports.conclusion: Second-degree AV block, Mobitz I (Wenckebach), ventricular rate 38.

documents.title: Emergency department physician record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital emergency department. Received by fax 04/09/2024. Date of service 04/06/2024.

CC: passed out at home.
HPI: 70M with CAD (LAD stent 2020), HTN, on metoprolol, who went down while walking from the living room to the kitchen this evening. Brief, came to on the floor; no seizure activity, no incontinence, no head strike per patient. Called his daughter, who called EMS. Felt washed out but no chest pain or shortness of breath.
Meds per patient list: aspirin, atorvastatin, lisinopril, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, mirtazapine nightly, acetaminophen prn.
Allergies: NKDA.
Exam on arrival: pulse 38, BP 88/60, RR 16. Awake and alert, tired looking. Heart sounds distant, no murmur; lungs clear. Remainder of cardiopulmonary exam unremarkable. No injuries.
ECG: Mobitz I second-degree AV block, rate 38.
Labs: hs-troponin I normal x2. Potassium normal. Creatinine normal. Hemoglobin normal.
Course: placed on telemetry with pads on. Metoprolol held. Rate came up to the 50s-60s overnight without intervention; no higher-grade block on telemetry. BP normalized.
Impression: syncope due to symptomatic second-degree AV block, Mobitz type I, likely aggravated by beta blocker.
Disposition: discharged 04/07. STOP metoprolol. Follow up with cardiology within 2 weeks and with PCP this week. Return for recurrent lightheadedness or fainting.

documents.title: Patient call after ED visit

documents.body: Pt called: fainted at home Saturday, ED said his heart rate was too slow and "took me off the metoprolol." Home since Sunday morning. No further spells, no dizziness. Has a cardiology appt 4/19. Advised no driving until cleared and to sit or lie down for any lightheadedness. ED records requested. Post-ED visit Friday 4/12 with PCP.

Seen after the ED visit 4/6 (record received 4/9 and reviewed). Collapsed at home, ED found Mobitz I with a rate in the 30s and soft pressure; troponin normal, rate recovered off metoprolol.

Since home: no further episodes, no lightheadedness. Has not taken metoprolol since. Chest pressure once this week walking the dog, eased with rest. Mood steady.
Exam: vitals reviewed, pulse regular today. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. No edema. No bruising or injury from the fall.

A/P:

2. CAD/stable angina: on aspirin, statin, lisinopril. Watch for more angina off the beta blocker; cardiology to weigh in.
3. HTN: fine today.

Outside cardiology group, visits 04/19/2024 and 05/14/2024.
Seen after his ED visit for syncope with Mobitz I AV block. Off metoprolol since 4/6, he has had no further syncope or presyncope and the ECG in clinic shows sinus rhythm with 1:1 conduction. We attribute the Wenckebach to beta blockade and will keep him off it. He may drive.
He notes his exertional chest pressure is somewhat more frequent since metoprolol was stopped, still with exertion and relieved by rest.
Medications: aspirin 81 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, lisinopril 20 mg, mirtazapine 30 mg, acetaminophen prn. No beta blocker. NKDA.
Plan: exercise treadmill stress test to reassess ischemic burden; we will decide on catheterization based on the result. Avoid AV-nodal blocking agents.

reports.text:
EXERCISE TREADMILL TEST (outside cardiology)
Indication: stable angina, more frequent off beta blocker.
Protocol: Bruce. Baseline ECG: sinus rhythm, normal conduction.
The patient exercised to near-target heart rate and stopped for typical chest pressure at peak exercise. Horizontal ST depression developed at peak and resolved in recovery, along with the chest pressure. Blood pressure response normal. No arrhythmia or conduction abnormality during exercise or recovery.
reports.conclusion: Positive for exercise-induced ischemia with typical angina. No arrhythmia. Findings consistent with his stable angina; elective coronary angiography recommended.

conditions.label: Anaphylactoid reaction to iodinated contrast media

documents.title: Cardiac catheterization procedure note
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Outside cardiology, cardiac catheterization laboratory. Procedure date 09/30/2024. Received 10/03/2024.

Procedure planned: elective left heart catheterization and coronary angiography.
Indication: stable angina with positive exercise treadmill test 09/05/2024; CAD with prior MI and LAD drug-eluting stent (2020).
Pre-procedure: alert, comfortable, no chest pain. No known drug allergies. Home medications: aspirin 81 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, lisinopril 20 mg, mirtazapine 30 mg, acetaminophen prn. Not on a beta blocker since 04/2024.

Event: Arterial access obtained without difficulty. Shortly after the first contrast injection the patient abruptly became flushed and hypotensive and then obtunded. Temperature 36.9 C, HR 118, BP 78/40, RR 26, SpO2 95% on room air. Tachycardic, skin warm and diffusely erythematous, bounding peripheral pulses. No JVD, no rales, no peripheral edema. No urticaria, no wheeze, no stridor.
Assessment: anaphylactoid reaction to iodinated contrast.
Management: contrast stopped and the procedure aborted before diagnostic images were complete. IV epinephrine, rapid IV fluid boluses, IV diphenhydramine and IV methylprednisolone. Mental status and blood pressure recovered over about 20 minutes. Sheath removed, hemostasis achieved.
Post-procedure: observed overnight on telemetry; no recurrence, no arrhythmia. Discharged 10/01 in good condition.

Plan: iodinated contrast allergy added, severe. Any future contrast study requires steroid and antihistamine premedication with an anesthesia team available. Coronary anatomy not defined; continue medical management of angina for now and review in clinic.

documents.title: Heart cath
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Doc, I guess you heard the cath didn't go well. I had a bad reaction to the dye and they had to stop. They said I'm allergic now. Does that mean no more scans? I have my lung CT next month.

documents.title: RE: Heart cath
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Paul, I read the report and I'm glad you came through it. I've added the contrast dye allergy to your chart as severe. Your lung screening CT uses no dye at all, so that is safe to keep. If you ever need a test with dye in the future it can still be done, with medicines given beforehand to prevent a reaction; always tell anyone doing a scan or a procedure about this allergy. Cardiology will see you to plan next steps for the chest pressure.

documents.title: Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Ten weeks after the aborted cath (contrast reaction). Fully recovered from that. Chest pressure about weekly with exertion, sometimes twice, always settles with rest within minutes; no rest pain, no syncope, no palpitations. Sees cardiology early January to decide on next steps. Mood good, PHQ-9 5.
Exam: vitals reviewed. Heart regular, lungs clear, no edema.
A/P: stable angina, more frequent off beta blocker, cardiology managing; told him to call or go to the ED for chest pain at rest or lasting more than 15 minutes. HTN controlled on lisinopril. Contrast allergy on file. MDD partial remission, continue mirtazapine. RTC 3 months.
